0x3F6E511507A082B3DBFC955480EA97D33F3488.motivation:
WakeUp Labs is a software development company providing services for EVM-compatible chains, DAOs, protocols, and startups. We are committed to driving the growth of the web3 ecosystem and Ethereum by upholding our core values of decentralization, collaboration, and excellence.

Since February, we have been increasingly involved with the Arbitrum DAO.

During this time, through collaboration with several delegates, we identified a need among users: an escape mechanism from the ARB chain in case the sequencer is not functioning properly. We made our first formal proposal to the DAO, which was one of the few that passed through the DAO’s mechanism without intermediaries and involved direct implementation, receiving 99.47% support from voters.

Our involvement has continued to grow, with contributions on the forum, at events such as ETHDenver, EthCC in Brussels, and local conferences like ETH Argentina and Aleph (Pop-up city). We have successfully contributed to the Arbitrum SDK, providing code improvements without any direct contracts with Off-Chain Labs or the Foundation, further proving our commitment to the ecosystem.

We are motivated to join the Security Council because we believe it’s a critical role within the DAO, one that we are equipped to fulfill due to our technical expertise, geographic diversity, and proven communication skills. Our team has the knowledge, dedication, and responsibility to serve in this capacity, with the aim of supporting Arbitrum’s mission and upholding the council’s integrity.

Gonzacolo, our co-founder and representative, has dedicated significant time and resources to researching the ARB ecosystem, actively participating in forums, and sharing our technical perspective on proposals that align with the community’s values.

As a team based in Argentina, we contribute geographic decentralization and bring unique insights to the table, along with our extensive experience in technical software development.

We also excel in communication—an area often lacking in DAOs—demonstrated through our clear, detailed proposals and project follow-ups.

As part of the Security Council, we will provide transparent communication about council decisions, engaging with the community via forums and social media to explain key issues and decisions in depth.

Representing WakeUp Labs as a team rather than an individual allows us to allocate more time to thoroughly research each proposal, ensuring the professionalism and quality that the role demands.

We are committed to being a responsible and active participant on the Security Council, aligned with the values of decentralization and dedicated to enhancing the Arbitrum ecosystem.

0x913Af9a61d1a59aA5D21CE9Bbf7Fd44Ed61dB4.experience:
I am Pablo Sabbatella, also known as pablito.eth. I am a web3 operational security researcher, member of SEAL (Security Alliance) and I am applying for the security council as founder of Opsek. I also created “Blockchain Security series” podcast.

I started with cybersecurity back in 1999, when I founded Hackemate and have been involved in technology since then. I am part of the Optimism Security Council and the Polygon Protocol Council.

I founded Opsek, where we do operational security audits and training for Web3 organizations (DeFi, CEXs, L1s, L2s, VCs, service providers and HNWI). The reason behind my work and founding Opsek is very simple: 99% of funds being lost are due to operational security issues (Private key leakage, malware, exploits, social engineering, phishing, account takeovers, domain hijacking, etc) and not due to smart contract hacks anymore.
My expertise is understanding an organization, defining and protecting its attack surface: what does the organization do? Who is the team? What are the tools and tack that they use? What does the day to day operation look like? What are the most valuable assets it’s protecting? Which are the biggest risks? We also train the teams on physical security.
Part of our auditing process includes multisigs: how were they created? Who are the signers? What’s the appropriate threshold? How are private keys generated? How are seeds handled? Are they backed up or deleted? How do you travel with your hardware wallet? Have signers developed a threat model? Hardware wallet diversity, frontend diversity, transactions verification and simulation, definition of procedures and policies, etc.

I have already audited many firms (many of them we do not make public). Some of them: Optimism, Sky (ex MakerDao), Centrifuge, Contango, Midas, Aligned Layer, and many more.
I have participated in many war rooms and helped many people and companies save funds during attacks (and still do this daily).
